title: The Lock Nobody Holds

post.author: u/lane_bakehouse_halinka
post.title: I keep the keys to our church tower. At three this morning the bell struck six, and the tower's log says two machines held the one lock.

blocks.text: I'm Halinka. From half past two I bake for the village shop, across the lane from Tolbeck church, and I'm the tower's volunteer bell-keeper. The clock has struck every hour, day and night, since 1873; in 2019 the village voted to keep the night strikes.
Since April 2024 a motor lifts the bell's hammer, worked by two small computers called controllers. A rings the hours. B, a spare, stays switched on, so the hour still rings if A dies.

Only one may ring an hour, so each must first hold the lock: a permission one holder has at a time, like a room's single key. The lock lives on three more small computers, lock servers 1, 2 and 3. A server's yes is called a grant.

Taking the lock goes in steps. A controller asks server 1, then 2, then 3, and stops at two yeses: more than half, a majority. With fewer, it hands them back and stays quiet. With two, it rings. Each grant lasts 60 seconds, its lifetime; then the server forgets it.
A asks two seconds before the hour, to have the lock at the stroke. B asks one second after; normally servers 1 and 2 still hold A's grants, so B hands back its one yes.
The servers keep grants in memory, the part of a computer that is wiped when it restarts: it stops, then starts again empty. Nothing goes on their disk, the part that keeps things with the power off.
Each line of the tower's log shows the time, who acted, and what happened. The last column is the token: a number some lock systems hand out with each grant, one higher each time. Ours give none.

02:59:58  A         asks  server 1 yes  server 2 yes                holds 2 of 3  token -
02:59:59  server 2  restarts
03:00:00  A         strikes
03:00:01  server 2  back, memory empty
03:00:01  B         asks  server 1 no   server 2 yes  server 3 yes  holds 2 of 3  token -
03:00:01  B         strikes
03:00:03  A         strikes
03:00:04  B         strikes
03:00:06  A         strikes
03:00:07  B         strikes
From 02:59:59 until B asked, by the servers' count, nobody held the lock. A rang anyway.

I heard it at my kneading table: three o'clock struck twice over, a second apart. Then my phone: Mr Sedgecombe from the forge cottage, then Mechtild at the old post house, asking if the clock had broken.

I rang the night line of Beaufoy Turret Clocks, who look after our clock. Darragh, their engineer on call, had pushed an update, a new version of the lock servers' program, at 02:59. Its makers had warned of a flaw letting strangers online give the servers orders, so he marked it urgent: install at once.
The update restarts one server every ten minutes, server 2 first. Its restart took 2 seconds, and it came back knowing nothing. A's grant on server 1 ran to 03:00:58, but one grant is not two.

Server 2 holds A's grant from 02:59:58, restarts from 02:59:59 to 03:00:01, then holds a grant for B. Server 3 holds no grant until 03:00:01, then a grant for B. Markers: 02:59:58 A gets servers 1 and 2; 02:59:59 server 2 restarts; 03:00:00 A rings; 03:00:01 B gets servers 2 and 3.

Server 2 restarted at 02:59:59 and was back, empty, at 03:00:01, when B got servers 2 and 3. A struck at 03:00:00, :03 and :06; B at 03:00:01, :04 and :07.

blocks.text: Updates normally install at 14:30, when no lock is held: a lock lives from two seconds before the hour to a minute after. In eleven updates since 2024, no server restarted holding a grant.
Beaufoy has switched off the night strikes until the parish council meets on Monday 14 December. What should I tell it to change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Every lock across machines rests on one promise: any two majorities of the same three servers share a server, and that server, already holding the first grant, says no to the second. Before you choose, test the promise against your log. Which server did A's grant and B's grant share? What did that server remember at 03:00:01? Would it have mattered if server 3 had restarted instead, or server 1? And when B's first strike reached the motor, could the motor tell anything about whose lock it came from?

replies.author: u/lane_bakehouse_halinka
replies.text: They shared server 2, and it remembered nothing. Server 3 held nothing for A, so its restart would have changed nothing. Server 1 restarting would have handed B servers 1 and 3 instead. The motor obeys any strike from either controller; it can't tell them apart.

comments.author: u/more_nodes_eadric
comments.text: A majority of lock servers is already safe; that's the whole point of a majority. Two majorities of three must share a server, so they can't both exist, unless one of the three goes missing, and three is simply too few to ride that out. Add servers. With five, B needs three yeses, and one restart can't hand it three. Same design, two more small computers, done before Monday.

replies.author: u/lane_bakehouse_halinka
replies.text: Darragh likes this: two more servers fit on the clock-room shelf, a morning's work. The council's chair has her own idea: make each grant last 5 minutes instead of 60 seconds, so a lock outlasts any restart.

comments.author: u/quiet_minute_gervase
comments.text: I look after lock servers like yours at work. The makers of Redis, a popular program often used for exactly this, describe your night in their own guide, and their answer needs no new machines: after any restart, a lock server stays silent for a little longer than the lifetime, here just over 60 seconds, before it answers anyone. By then every grant it forgot has run out on its own, so it can't give out a second.

reply.prompt: The parish council meets on Monday 14 December. What should Halinka tell it to change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Spread the lock over five lock servers instead of three, so one restart cannot matter.
options.part2: Beaufoy fitted servers 4 and 5 on Wednesday 16 December, and the night strikes came back. In the sim, replaying 10 December with five: A asks servers 1, 2 and 3 and stops at three yeses, a majority of five. Server 2 restarts at 02:59:59 and comes back empty. At 03:00:01 B asks: server 1 no, server 2 yes, server 3 no, servers 4 and 5 yes. Three of five, a second majority, and six strokes. On Tuesday 19 January 2027 another urgent update went out at 02:59; Darragh pushed it straight away, trusting five servers to cover a restart. Server 2 restarted at 02:59:59, and Mr Sedgecombe rang me at 03:01 to say he had counted six.
options.senior: A majority protects you only while every server that said yes still remembers saying it. Five servers raise how many yeses a lock needs, but a holder that stops at a bare majority, three of five, leaves two servers free, and one forgetful restart among its three makes three again for the next asker. Redis's own guide gives exactly this case with five servers. More servers let you ride out servers that are down; they do nothing about servers that forget. Make grants survive a restart, or keep a restarted server out until its grants would have run out.

options.text: Lengthen the lock's lifetime from 60 seconds to 5 minutes, so it outlasts any restart.
options.part2: On Wednesday 16 December Darragh set every grant to last 300 seconds, and the night strikes came back. In the sim, replaying 10 December: A's grants now run to 03:04:58, but server 2's restart wipes its copy all the same, and at 03:00:01 B gets servers 2 and 3. Six strokes. On Tuesday 19 January 2027 another urgent update restarted server 2 at 02:59:59, and Mechtild rang me at 03:01: six again.
options.senior: A lifetime is how long a server promises to remember a grant, and a restart that wipes memory breaks the promise however long it was. Lengthening it changes nothing about a server that forgets, and it costs you: when a holder really dies, everyone waits out the longer lifetime before the lock can be taken again. Keep lifetimes as short as the work allows, and make the grant itself survive a restart.

options.text: Keep the lock on servers that save each grant to disk, with a token the motor checks.
options.part2: Beaufoy replaced the three lock servers with etcd, a lock service built on consensus: three servers that agree by majority, each writing every grant to its disk before it answers and reading it back after a restart. With each lock it hands out a token, one higher each time, and the bell motor now refuses a strike carrying a lower token than the last it obeyed. In the sim, replaying 10 December: A gets the lock with token 1; server 2 restarts at 02:59:59 and reloads A's grant from disk; at 03:00:01 B gets one yes of three and stays quiet. Three strokes. On Tuesday 19 January 2027 another urgent update restarted server 2 at 02:59:59, and I counted three at my kneading table. Darragh now checks the clock before he pushes anything urgent, too.
options.senior: A lock across machines is only as safe as the servers' memory of who holds it. Build it on a consensus service such as etcd or ZooKeeper: a grant counts only once a majority has written it to disk, so a restarted server comes back knowing what it promised, and two majorities can never both say yes. Then hand out a token that only goes up, and make the thing being protected check it, because even a correct lock can't stop a holder that froze past its lifetime from acting late, the lesson of It Didn't Know It Was Dead. The lock keeps two holders apart; the token stops the late one.

options.text: Make a restarted lock server stay silent for longer than a lock's 60-second lifetime.
options.verdict: Trade-off: fixes tonight, no token, a silent hour
options.part2: On Wednesday 16 December Darragh set every lock server to stay silent for 62 seconds after it goes down, just over the lifetime. In the sim, replaying 10 December: server 2 is back at 03:00:01 but silent until 03:01:01, so B gets one yes of three and stays quiet. Three strokes, and no token: the motor still can't tell an old holder from a new one. On Tuesday 19 January 2027 another urgent update restarted server 2 at 02:59:59, and the hour struck three. Then, on Thursday 4 February, the power strip all three lock servers share tripped at 02:59:55 for 2 seconds. All three came back silent until 03:00:57, A got no answers at 02:59:58, and three o'clock did not strike at all. In the sim, the same trip without the delayed restart still gives three strokes.
options.senior: Delayed restarts are real and documented: Redis's guide says a restarted server that stays away for a bit more than the longest lifetime can't take part in any lock that was live when it went down, so the scheme stays safe without saving to disk. The price is availability: if a majority restarts together, nobody can take any lock for a whole lifetime. And it still hands out no token, so a holder that froze past its lifetime can still act late, and the whole fix leans on every server timing its silence correctly. A sound patch for tonight's hole; a consensus service with tokens closes it without the patch.

sim.title: Replay three o'clock on the lock servers
sim.lede: You're Halinka, replaying Thursday 10 December 2026 from 02:59:50 to 03:01:00 in one-second steps. As given data: three lock servers keep grants in memory, each for a 60-second lifetime. A controller asks server 1, then 2, then 3 (then 4 and 5), and stops at a majority; a server that is down or silent gives no answer, one already holding a live grant says no, and with fewer than a majority the controller hands back what it got. A, the main controller, asks at 02:59:58; B, the spare, at 03:00:01. A holder rings three strokes, one every 3 seconds, from the hour or from when it got the lock if later. The urgent update restarts server 2 at 02:59:59 for 2 seconds. Saved to disk: each server writes each grant to disk before it answers and reloads it after a restart, and the service's counter gives each lock a token one higher than the last. The motor's token check refuses a stroke whose token is lower than the last it obeyed. A delayed restart keeps a restarted server silent until the lifetime plus 2 seconds after it went down. Instead of the update, the power strip that all the lock servers share can trip.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as on the night: A holds servers 1 and 2, server 2 forgets, B gets 2 and 3, six strokes. Step to 03:00:00: by the servers' count nobody holds the lock, and A strikes. Five servers: B gets 2, 4 and 5. Lifetime 300 s: still six. Token check alone: there is no token to check. Saved to disk: B refused, three strokes, token 1; then a 2 s lifetime: B gets the lock with token 2 and the motor refuses A's last two strokes. Delayed restart: three strokes, no token; then trip the power strip at 02:59:55: no strokes at all.

explain.oneLine: Nobody broke the lock's rule; one of its servers forgot. At 02:59:58 A held servers 1 and 2. A second later an update wiped server 2's memory, and at 03:00:01 B found two servers holding nothing: a second majority, and six strokes. Keep grants where a restart can't lose them, on a consensus service that saves each one to disk, and let the motor check a token.

steps.title: Taking a lock across machines, in steps.
steps.text: On one machine a lock is a marker in that machine's memory (s5e01). Across machines there is no shared memory, so the lock becomes a vote. First, the controller asks each lock server for a grant; a server already holding a live grant says no. Second, it counts the yeses; servers can be slow or down, so it needs only a majority, 2 of 3. Third, it acts only with that majority; with fewer, it hands back what it got. Fourth, the grants expire after their lifetime, so a controller that dies holding the lock can't silence the tower for good. The safety rests on one fact: any two majorities of the same servers share a server, and that server, holding the first grant, refuses the second.

steps.title: A server that forgets breaks the shared server.
steps.text: At 02:59:58 A asked server 1, then 2, and stopped at two yeses, each good to 03:00:58. At 02:59:59 the urgent update restarted server 2: it stopped, its memory was wiped, and it was back at 03:00:01 knowing nothing. For those two seconds the servers held one grant for A, so by their count nobody held the lock, while A, which never checks again once it has the lock, rang at 03:00:00. At 03:00:01 B asked: server 1 said no, server 2 had nothing to defend and said yes, and so did server 3. The server the two majorities shared was server 2, and it had forgotten. It never showed before because updates installed at 14:30, when no lock is held.

steps.title: More servers, a longer lifetime: the same hole.
steps.text: With five servers A stops at three yeses, 1, 2 and 3; server 2 forgets, and B gets 2, 4 and 5. Redis's guide gives this very case with five. A 5-minute lifetime is a longer promise that server 2 forgot just the same. Asking every server instead of stopping at a majority would have saved tonight, but whenever one server is slow to answer the holder again has a bare majority, and one forgetful restart undoes it.

steps.title: A lock service that never forgets, and a token at the motor.
steps.text: etcd and ZooKeeper keep a small shared record on three or five servers that agree by consensus. A grant counts only once a majority has written it to disk, and a restarted server reads its disk back before it answers anyone. So server 2 would have come back still holding A's grant, and B would have been refused. Each lock also comes with a number that only goes up, which etcd calls a revision. The motor keeps the highest number it has obeyed and refuses a lower one: the fencing token of It Didn't Know It Was Dead, which guards against a holder that outlived its lock, not a service that forgot. What can still go wrong: if a majority of the service's servers is down or cut off, nobody gets the lock, and the hour stays silent.

steps.title: The Redlock debate, fairly.
steps.text: Redlock is Redis's lock over several independent servers, the design Tolbeck's servers copy. In February 2016 Martin Kleppmann argued that its safety rests on timing assumptions and that it gives no fencing token, so locks that guard correctness belong on a consensus system such as ZooKeeper. Salvatore Sanfilippo, Redis's author, who writes as antirez, replied that a unique random value per lock can do the token's job and that delayed restarts or saving to disk cover restarts, so it is safe as long as each server can count time with a bounded error.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for 10 December. Controller A asks the lock service at 02:59:58 and is granted the lock with token 1. At 02:59:59 server 2 restarts and reloads A's grant from its disk. A strikes with token 1 and the motor obeys. At 03:00:01 controller B asks and is told no, the lock is held by A. Outcome: three strokes, all with token 1.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 10 December. Server 2 still restarts at 02:59:59, but it wrote A's grant to disk before answering, so it comes back holding it. When B asks at 03:00:01 the service says no, and the motor hears only A, with token 1.

fix.title: The fix: a lock service that saves every grant, and a token the motor checks
fix.text: Move the lock to a consensus service such as etcd: three servers that agree by majority, where a grant counts only once a majority has written it to disk, and a restarted server reads its grants back before it answers. Keep the 60-second lifetime, so a controller that dies still lets go. With each lock the service hands out a token that only goes up; each strike carries it, and the bell motor remembers the highest token it has obeyed and refuses a lower one. And treat an urgent update like any other change: check what the machines are doing first, and never restart a lock server in the minutes around an hour.

limits: The service keeps two holders apart; it can't stop a late one. A controller that freezes past its lifetime still believes it holds the lock, and only the motor's token check stops its strikes. Anything that acts without checking the token stays unprotected.
It needs a majority of its servers up and in touch. Lose two of three together and nobody can take the lock, so the hour goes unrung: the safe way to fail, and still a failure the parish will hear.
Writing to disk before answering makes each grant a little slower, and a disk that claims a write is finished before it really is can still lose a grant in a power cut.

explain.seniorTake: A lock across machines is a vote, and a vote is only as good as the voters' memory. A majority is safe because any two majorities share a voter who refuses the second request; a server that restarts with an empty memory is a voter with no memory of its vote, and one is enough to build a second majority. More servers and longer lifetimes don't touch that. Put locks that matter on a consensus service such as etcd or ZooKeeper, which writes each grant to disk on a majority before answering, and accept that it refuses when it can't reach a majority. Then fence: hand out a number that only goes up and make the thing being protected refuse an older one, because no lock service can stop a holder that froze past its lifetime. Use a faster lock without these only where two holders now and then would be harmless, and treat an urgent restart of anything holding state as a change, not a reflex.

realWorld.title: Redis's guide: Redlock in steps
realWorld.text: Redis's own page on distributed locks describes taking a lock on several independent servers: "If and only if the client was able to acquire the lock in the majority of the instances (at least 3), and the total time elapsed to acquire the lock is less than lock validity time, the lock is considered to be acquired." Its example uses five servers.

realWorld.title: Redis's guide: tonight, with five servers
realWorld.text: The same page describes Tolbeck's night: "A client acquires the lock in 3 of 5 instances. One of the instances where the client was able to acquire the lock is restarted, at this point there are again 3 instances that we can lock for the same resource, and another client can lock it again, violating the safety property of exclusivity of lock." That is why five servers were no fix.

realWorld.title: Redis's guide: delayed restarts, and their price
realWorld.text: Its answer without saving to disk: "To guarantee this we just need to make an instance, after a crash, unavailable for at least a bit more than the max TTL we use." TTL, short for time to live, is the lifetime. And: "Using delayed restarts it is basically possible to achieve safety even without any kind of Redis persistence available, however note that this may translate into an availability penalty."

realWorld.title: Kleppmann, 8 February 2016: the token, and the restart
realWorld.text: Martin Kleppmann's essay defines the fencing token: "In this context, a fencing token is simply a number that increases (e.g. incremented by the lock service) every time a client acquires the lock." On Redlock and restarts: "A similar issue could happen if C crashes before persisting the lock to disk, and immediately restarts." His advice for locks that guard correctness: "Instead, please use a proper consensus system such as ZooKeeper".

realWorld.title: antirez, February 2016: the reply
realWorld.text: Redis's author answered in "Is Redlock safe?". On the token, he argues that "a unique identifier for each lock can be used for the same goals, but is much more practical". On restarts, that with Redlock "you can opt-out any disk involvement at all by implementing delayed restarts". And on his own question: "So is Redlock safe or not? It depends on the above."

realWorld.title: ZooKeeper: to disk before it counts
realWorld.text: ZooKeeper's overview says its servers keep their record in memory but "writes are serialized to disk before they are applied to the in-memory database." Among its guarantees: "Once an update has been applied, it will persist from that time forward".

realWorld.title: etcd: the lock is not the whole fence
realWorld.text: etcd's comparison page is blunt about its own locks: "The lock APIs cannot be used as mutual exclusion mechanism by themselves." It maps Kleppmann's token onto etcd's ever-growing record number: "The authors interpret that fencing token is revision number in the case of etcd."

asked: How would you build a lock across several machines?
What goes wrong with Redlock when a server restarts?
Why does a lock need a fencing token?
interview.answer: First I'd ask what the lock protects. If two holders now and then would only waste work, a single Redis key with an expiry is fine. If two holders would do harm, I'd use a consensus service such as etcd or ZooKeeper. Taking the lock goes in steps: ask the servers, count the yeses, act only with a majority, and let the lock expire after a lifetime so a dead holder can't block everyone. It's safe because any two majorities share a server that refuses the second request, but only if that server remembers. Redlock keeps locks on independent Redis servers, by default in memory; if one that said yes restarts with its memory wiped, a second client can gather a fresh majority while the first still believes it holds the lock. Redis's guide shows exactly this with 3 of 5 servers and offers saving to disk on every write, or delayed restarts: a restarted server stays silent for longer than any lock's lifetime. A consensus service writes each grant to disk on a majority before answering, so it never forgets. Even then, a holder can freeze past its lifetime and act late, so the lock service hands out a fencing token, a number that only goes up, and the resource refuses any token lower than the newest it has seen. I'd tell the story of a church tower where an urgent update restarted one of three memory-only lock servers a second after it granted the lock, and three o'clock struck six.

terms.def: The tower in this story. Its clock has struck every hour, day and night, since 1873; since April 2024 a motor worked by two controllers lifts the bell's hammer.
The volunteer who holds the tower's keys and is called when something is wrong. Halinka, who lives across the lane, is Tolbeck's.
The firm that looks after Tolbeck's clock, its controllers and its lock servers. Darragh is its engineer on call at night.
One blow of the hammer on the bell. Three o'clock is three strokes; at Tolbeck they come 3 seconds apart.
A small computer that works the bell motor. Tolbeck has two: A rings the hours, B is a spare that stays switched on and asks for the lock a second after the hour.
The motor that lifts and drops the hammer. It obeys a strike from either controller; in the fix, only if the strike's token is not lower than the last it obeyed.
A permission only one holder may have at a time, like the single key to a room (s5e01). At Tolbeck, a controller must hold it before ringing.
A lock kept on several machines instead of one, so it survives one of them failing. A holder needs a majority of them to agree.
A small computer that hands out a lock and remembers who holds it. Tolbeck has three, 1, 2 and 3; a controller needs two of them.
A lock server's yes to one controller, kept for the lock's lifetime. A server holding a live grant says no to anyone else.
More than half of the servers: 2 of 3, 3 of 5. Any two majorities of the same servers share at least one.
How long a server keeps a grant before forgetting it on its own: 60 seconds at Tolbeck. Redis calls it the TTL, short for time to live.
The part of a computer that holds what it is working on. It is wiped when the computer restarts or loses power.
The part of a computer that keeps things with the power off. A grant written there survives a restart.
Stopping a program or computer and starting it again: it stops, its memory is wiped, and it starts again knowing only what was on its disk (s5e02).
A new version of a program, installed by restarting it. Beaufoy's tool installs on one lock server every ten minutes, normally from 14:30.
An update marked to install at once instead of at the usual time. Darragh pushed one at 02:59 to close a flaw that let strangers give the servers orders.
A number handed out with each lock, one higher each time (s8e02). Whatever acts keeps the highest it has seen and refuses a lower one.
The protected thing, here the bell motor, refusing any request whose token is lower than the newest it has obeyed, so a late holder can't act.
Several servers agreeing on one record even when some fail, like a vote that never goes back on its result (s8e04).
A lock kept by servers that agree by majority and write each grant to disk before answering, so no restart makes them forget it.
An open-source program that keeps a small record on several servers that agree by consensus (s8e04). It offers locks, with a revision number usable as a token.
An open-source coordination service that keeps a small shared record on several servers, the other common choice beside etcd (s8e04).
etcd's number for every change to its record, from one counter that only goes up. It can serve as a lock's fencing token.
A popular open-source program that keeps data in memory for speed, often used for locks. It can also save to disk, at some cost in speed.
Redis's design for a lock on several independent Redis servers: take it on a majority within the lifetime. Tolbeck's lock servers work the same way.
Saving data to disk so it survives a restart. fsync is the call that makes a computer finish writing to disk before it carries on.
A restarted lock server staying silent for a little longer than the longest lifetime, so every grant it forgot has run out before it answers.
Whether a system can do its job right now. A delayed restart trades some away: while servers are silent, nobody may get a lock.
A row of sockets fed by one plug. All three of Tolbeck's lock servers share one, so one trip takes them down together.
A program stopping for a while without knowing it, then carrying on as if no time had passed (s8e02). A holder can freeze past its lifetime.
A researcher in distributed systems whose 2016 essay How to do distributed locking argued that Redlock is unsafe for locks that guard correctness.
The online name of Salvatore Sanfilippo, who wrote Redis and Redlock. His 2016 post Is Redlock safe? answered Kleppmann.
The village's elected council. It decides what Tolbeck's clock does, and voted in 2019 to keep the night strikes.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A 8.14 covers redundancy of systems; A 8.32 covers change management.
Deciding, recording and checking every change to a system before it is made, urgent ones included, so its effect on running work is known.

atWork: Look for places where several copies of a program take a lock before doing something that must happen once: a nightly job on two machines, a queue worker that elects a leader, a payment step guarded by a key with an expiry. Read-only access is enough. First, list every lock that lives on another machine: Redis keys set with an expiry, Redlock libraries, locks kept inside a database, and locks in etcd or ZooKeeper. Second, for each one, ask what its servers remember after a restart. If they run Redis, `CONFIG GET appendonly` and `CONFIG GET appendfsync` show whether grants are written to disk and how often; check too whether automatic updates or restarts can happen while locks are held. Third, ask what the protected thing does when two holders act: does it check a fencing token, or does it trust whoever arrives? Where two holders would do harm, move the lock to a consensus service and pass its token to the place that acts. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 8.32 (change management) expects changes, urgent ones included, to follow a controlled process, which should include checking what a restart interrupts; and A 8.14 (redundancy of information processing facilities) expects redundancy that actually meets your availability needs, which three servers that forget on restart do not. Flag for the design: a lock that guards money or a physical action and rests on memory-only servers would need rework before an audit that relies on it, so build it on a consensus service with fencing from the first design.

recall.prompt: Your company runs its nightly billing job on two machines. To stop both sending invoices, each takes a lock from three lock servers before it starts and needs two of the three to say yes. Last night every customer got two invoices. The logs show that one lock server restarted for an automatic update a few seconds after the first machine began. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The restarted server forgot the first machine's grant, so the second machine could gather a second majority
Keep the lock on a consensus service that writes every grant to disk on a majority before answering, such as etcd or ZooKeeper
Pass a fencing token to the invoice sender, which refuses any token lower than the newest it has seen

recall.model: The lock server that restarted kept its grants only in memory, so it forgot the first machine's grant and came back empty. When the second machine asked, that server and the third said yes: a second majority while the first still believed it held the lock, so both sent invoices. I'd move the lock to a consensus service such as etcd or ZooKeeper, which writes every grant to disk on a majority before answering, so a restart never forgets. And I'd pass the lock's fencing token to the invoice sender, which refuses any token lower than the newest it has seen, so a holder that froze past its lifetime can't send late.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with everything else as on the night, which single change gives three strokes, B refused and a token issued to A?
options: Five lock servers instead of three
Grants saved to disk before answering
recall.why: Saved to disk, server 2 reloads A's grant after its restart, so B gets one yes of three and stays quiet; the service's counter gives A token 1. With five servers B gets 2, 4 and 5; with 300 s server 2 forgets anyway: six strokes both times. A delayed restart also gives three strokes, but hands out no token.

recall.prompt: Why can a lock that needs a majority of three memory-only lock servers end up with two holders?
options: Majorities of three are too small to share a server
A server that restarts forgets its grants, so the server two majorities share can say yes twice
The controllers' clocks disagree about when the hour starts
The lifetime was shorter than the restart
recall.why: Any two majorities of three share a server, and that server refuses the second request only if it remembers the first. Server 2 restarted with its memory wiped, so it said yes to B. The clocks and the 60-second lifetime played no part: server 2 was down for 2 seconds.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how would you build a lock across several machines, and why does it need a fencing token?

keyIdeas.idea: Grant the lock only with a majority of servers that agree by consensus and save each grant durably
The lock expires after a lifetime, so a dead holder can't block everyone
A holder can freeze past its lifetime and act late, so the resource refuses any number lower than the newest it has seen

recall.model: I'd use a consensus service such as etcd or ZooKeeper. A client asks the servers for the lock and gets it only when a majority agrees, and each grant is written to disk on that majority before the answer, so a restart can't make a server forget it. The lock expires after a lifetime, a lease, so a holder that dies can't block everyone forever. But a holder can freeze, in a long pause, past its lifetime and then act late, believing it still holds the lock. So with every lock the service hands out a number that only goes up, and the thing being protected keeps the newest it has seen and refuses any lower number.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The new lock service has held: since December every hour has struck right, through two more urgent updates. In February Beaufoy moved two of its three lock servers to their workshop, 30 km away, so its engineers could update them in their own building without climbing anything; the third stayed in the clock room, and the controllers reach the workshop over the tower's internet line. On the night of Monday 8 March 2027 a lorry brought down that line on our lane at 23:40, and it was mended at 05:20. The bell didn't strike midnight, or one, two, three, four or five. I noticed at three, at my kneading table. Darragh says the lock service did exactly what it should. Mr Sedgecombe says a bell that won't ring is broken.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the bell stay silent, should the lock service have refused, and where should Beaufoy put its servers?

keyIdeas.idea: The clock-room server alone is one of three, not a majority; cut off from the workshop's two, the service could grant nothing
Refusing was right: without a majority the service can't be sure nobody else holds the lock, so it chooses silence over two ringers
Put a majority where the bell is, two of three in the tower on separate power, so a cut line leaves the tower able to grant

coldCase.model: The clock-room server was one of three. Cut off from the two at the workshop, it was not a majority, so the service could grant nothing and neither controller could ring. It was right to refuse: without a majority it can't be sure that nobody else holds the lock, and a consensus service chooses silence over two ringers. That is by design, and it is safe. The mistake was where the servers went. Put the majority where the bell is: two of three in the tower, each on separate power, and the third at the workshop, so a cut line leaves the tower able to grant while the workshop alone can grant nothing. Keep the updates careful instead: one server at a time, never near an hour.
